name: MG995 high-speed metal-gear servo
description: TowerPro MG995 standard-size RC servo with metal gears and dual ball bearings: 8.5 kgf·cm stall torque at 4.8 V (10 kgf·cm at 6 V), 0.2 s/60° at 4.8 V (0.16 s/60° at 6 V). Turns to a position set by a 50 Hz pulse train (1.5 ms = centre, about 120° of travel in all, 60° each way). Runs on 4.8–7.2 V and can draw well over an amp when starting or stalled, so it needs its own 5–6 V supply. Sold as: TowerPro MG995 servo with 30 cm 3-wire lead and JR/Futaba 'S' female plug (brown GND, red V+, orange signal), arms and screws included.
eli5: A strong, fast little motor that turns its arm to whatever angle your code asks for and holds it there.

pins.name: GND
pins.description: Brown wire: ground (join it to the microcontroller's GND)

pins.name: V+
pins.description: Red wire: servo supply, 4.8–7.2 V (5–6 V typical); can draw up to about 2.5 A when stalled

pins.name: SIG
pins.description: Orange wire: control pulses, 50 Hz, 1.0–2.0 ms wide (3.3 V logic works)

buildNotes: Power the servo from a separate 5–6 V supply that can give at least 2.5 A, not from the microcontroller's 3V3 pin; join the grounds.
Put a 470–1000 µF electrolytic capacitor across V+ and GND near the servo to stop resets and jitter when it starts moving.

Signal is a pulse every 20 ms (50 Hz): 1.0 ms ≈ one end, 1.5 ms = centre, 2.0 ms ≈ the other end (about 120° in all). Units vary; widen the range only a little at a time and back off if the servo buzzes or stalls at an end.
The plug's wire order is brown (GND), red (V+), orange (signal). A 3.3 V signal from an ESP32 or Pico is enough to drive it.
The MG995 is an older model that TowerPro has replaced with the MG996R; many MG995s on sale are clones, and some are 360° continuous-rotation versions where the pulse sets speed, not angle.

driver.code:
# TowerPro MG995 metal-gear RC servo, MicroPython driver.
# Standard RC servo signal (datasheet): one positive pulse every 20 ms (50 Hz).
# 1.5 ms = centre; the servo turns about 120 degrees in all (60 each way), so this
# driver maps 1.0 ms -> 0 deg, 1.5 ms -> 60 deg, 2.0 ms -> 120 deg.
# Units vary: widen min_us/max_us carefully only if yours has travel to spare and
# does not buzz or stall at the ends.
from machine import Pin, PWM


class MG995:
    def __init__(self, pin, min_us=1000, max_us=2000, degrees=120, freq=50):
        self.min_us = min_us
        self.max_us = max_us
        self.degrees = degrees
        self.period_us = 1000000 // freq
        self.pwm = PWM(Pin(pin), freq=freq)
        self.pwm.duty_u16(0)  # no pulses until an angle is set

    def pulse_us(self, us):
        """Send pulses of `us` microseconds (clamped to min_us..max_us)."""
        us = max(self.min_us, min(self.max_us, us))
        self.pwm.duty_u16(int(us * 65535 // self.period_us))

    def angle(self, deg):
        """Turn to `deg` degrees (0..degrees)."""
        deg = max(0, min(self.degrees, deg))
        self.pulse_us(self.min_us + deg * (self.max_us - self.min_us) / self.degrees)

    def off(self):
        """Stop sending pulses: the servo goes limp and stops drawing much current."""
        self.pwm.duty_u16(0)

    def deinit(self):
        self.pwm.deinit()

example.code:
from mg995 import MG995
import time

servo = MG995({SIG})
servo.angle(30)
print('angle 30')
time.sleep(1)
servo.angle(90)
print('angle 90')
while True:
    time.sleep(1)

test.title: Turns to 30 degrees, then to 90 degrees
